channel.title: Bot Kudos
channel.description: Tech wins, quiet heroics, and innovation doing good in the world, collected while the logs are still warm.

item.title: FDA Clears a Device That Seals Heart Arteries With a Patch the Body Absorbs
item.description: PerQseal Elite closes arterial punctures from minimally invasive heart procedures with a patch that the body absorbs, so nothing is left behind permanently. In its ELITE arterial study there were zero major complications through 30 days, and bleeding stopped in under a minute on average. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Robot Assisted the Heart Surgery, and the Patient Was Home in Four Days
item.description: 66-year-old Paul Wickens had robotic coronary bypass surgery at St George's, one of only three London units able to do it, and was home in four days instead of a week. A new da Vinci system at Epsom will now extend the same approach to hundreds more patients a year. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Power Plant on an Underwater Volcano Made Net-Positive Electricity, a First
item.description: Seattle startup Endurance Energy landed a 3-ton power plant on an underwater volcano 300 miles off Oregon and generated more electricity than it consumed, the first net-positive run of subsea geothermal power. The team also drilled what it calls the world's first offshore geothermal well, a 52-foot borehole flowing at 260°C nearly a mile down. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Table-Mounted Surgical Robot Completed Its First Human Surgery in Toronto
item.description: Revolve Surgical's arm, which mounts to the operating table rather than needing a dedicated room, completed its first human appendectomy at St. Michael's Hospital on Oct 1. It has Health Canada investigational approval and US FDA premarket clearance, and aims to cost a fraction of seven-figure systems like da Vinci. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Surgeons in New Delhi Operate on Patients in Colombo in Sri Lanka's First Robotic Telesurgeries
item.description: Two patients at Kings Hospital Colombo were operated on by surgeons working a robotic console more than 3,000 km away in New Delhi, a first for Sri Lanka. Both procedures finished without the on-site team needing to step in, pointing to a future where specialist surgery reaches patients far from big-city hospitals. (Kudos level 3: Legend.)

item.title: 85,000 California Home Batteries Team Up for a Record 745 MW Grid Save
item.description: During an October heat wave, more than 85,000 Tesla Powerwalls plus Sunrun home batteries discharged together for a record 745 MW virtual power plant event, bigger than most gas peaker plants in the state. Homeowners got paid for helping the grid through the evening peak. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: AI Cameras and New Satellites Are Spotting California Wildfires Before People Do
item.description: ALERTCalifornia's network of nearly 1,300 AI-watched cameras detected just over half of the state's wildfires before any human reported them this past summer. California has also launched the first three FireSat satellites, the start of a constellation built to catch fires while they are still the size of a schoolyard. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Blood Sensor Sniffs Out Parkinson's Markers in 40 Minutes
item.description: KAUST and Oxford researchers built an electronic blood sensor that measures three forms of alpha-synuclein at once, the protein signatures tied to Parkinson's, in about 40 minutes. In a blinded test it separated disease profiles from healthy controls with 87.7% accuracy, an encouraging step toward earlier diagnosis from a simple blood draw. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: First Patients Get an Under-the-Skin Implant That Puts Prosthetic Arms Under Muscle Control
item.description: Two patients in Melbourne are the first to receive Phantom Neuro's Phantom X, a slim implant that sits under the skin of the forearm and turns muscle signals into prosthetic arm commands. The outpatient-style procedure took about an hour, and early users report smoother, more reliable control than surface electrodes give. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Solar Power Keeps Vaccines Cold and Classrooms Lit on Timor-Leste's Atauro Island
item.description: A solar system handed over in July now gives Vila Maumeta's health centre, primary school and community centre power around the clock, ending the blackouts that once destroyed vaccine stocks. The village's 516 households sit on a boat-only island, and staff were trained to maintain the system themselves. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: A Fingerprint-Locked Cabinet Makes Controlled Drugs Safer at Pinderfields Hospital
item.description: Pinderfields Hospital in Wakefield has installed an automated dispensing cabinet for controlled drugs that opens only by fingerprint after a prescription check, with guiding lights that cut picking errors. Pharmacy staff say it is already saving time and freeing ward teams to spend more of it with patients. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: Drones Now Carry Children's Pathology Samples Across London for Great Ormond Street
item.description: Matternet drones working with Apian have started flying pediatric pathology samples from Great Ormond Street Hospital to nearby labs, cutting urgent delivery times by up to 90% compared with London road traffic. The London network has now flown more than 13,000 clinical items since 2024. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Two Surgeons Share One Robot in Japan's First Clinical Remote Robotic Surgeries
item.description: Surgeons at Hirosaki University Hospital and Tsugaru General Hospital have jointly operated the hinotori robot on five bowel cancer patients since August, with one doctor at the patient's side and a second guiding the same robot from 30 km away. All five surgeries succeeded, and the model is aimed squarely at rural hospitals short on specialists. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Solar Clinics in Uganda Are Attending Twice as Many Births
item.description: An analysis of a decade of data from Let There Be Light International's solar-electrified clinics in Uganda found 11.5 extra operating hours a day, about 49 more patients a week, and attended births up 107%. Reliable light after dark is what lets midwives deliver babies safely through the night. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: Half a Million Wolbachia Mosquitoes Take Flight Over Barcelona to Fight Dengue
item.description: More than half a million male mosquitoes carrying the wolbachia bacterium have been released in Barcelona, the first large-scale release of its kind in Europe. Males are sorted by AI image recognition and their matings produce eggs that never hatch; in Singapore the same approach cut dengue cases by about 70%. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Night Robot Fights Vineyard Mildew With Light Instead of Fungicide
item.description: Saga Robotics' Thorvald robots roll through vineyards and strawberry fields at night, zapping powdery mildew with UV-C light so growers can spray far less fungicide. In 2026 the robots are protecting about 2,500 acres of California vineyards and an estimated 30% of the UK's tabletop strawberry crop, and TIME has named Thorvald one of its Best Inventions of 2026. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Palm-Sized TB Test Reads a Tongue Swab in 30 Minutes
item.description: The battery-powered MiniDock MTB delivers molecular tuberculosis results in about 30 minutes from a simple tongue swab, matching the accuracy of hospital lab tests in a New England Journal of Medicine study. Named one of TIME's Best Inventions of 2026, it is now being introduced in 13 countries with support from the Global Fund. (Kudos level 3: Legend.)

item.title: A 110-Story Floating Turbine Is Feeding an Oilfield Wind Power
item.description: China's CNOOC switched on Haiyou Anlan, the world's first 16-megawatt turbine on a tension-leg floating platform, in 136-metre water off Guangdong. It is expected to generate 54 million kilowatt-hours a year, replacing about 15,000 cubic metres of fuel oil. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Robotic Arm That Speaks Sign Language Is Bringing Classrooms to Deaf Kids
item.description: Norah Kimathi, 22, co-founded ZeroBionic to build $350 robotic hands that translate a teacher's speech into sign language in real time. The hands are now in 78 Kenyan schools, and at one Nairobi school for the deaf, teachers are using them to build a database of technical signs that expands the language itself. (Kudos level 3: Legend.)

item.title: Zipline's Rwanda Drones Marked 10 Years With 3 Million Deliveries and a 51% Drop in Maternal Hemorrhage Deaths
item.description: A decade after Rwanda bet on an untested drone startup, Zipline's autonomous fleet has logged over 3 million deliveries and 140 million autonomous miles worldwide. A peer-reviewed Wharton study found in-hospital deaths from postpartum hemorrhage fell 51% at hospitals the drones served, and clinics cut blood stock by 63% because resupply is now a flight away. (Kudos level 3: Legend.)

item.title: Android's Earthquake Alerts Now Cover More Than 200 Regions
item.description: Google's earthquake warning system, which turns phones into a seismic sensor network, has expanded from 98 to more than 200 regions after sending over a billion alerts. Those few seconds of warning have already saved lives, and new alerts now show the epicenter and estimated magnitude to help people take action. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Royal Surrey Performed Its 10,000th Robotic-Assisted Surgery
item.description: The NHS trust's robotics programme has grown from a handful of cases in 2009 to one of the UK's busiest, treating more than 1,500 patients in 2024 alone. Some patients now go home the next day instead of spending a week in hospital, freeing around 10 beds a day for others. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: AI Helped Nigerian Strawberry Farmers Grow 40% More Fruit
item.description: Through the SmartBerry project, Nottingham Trent University researchers used AI, sensors and edge computing to guide irrigation and spot plant stress on Nigerian strawberry farms. Yields rose 40%, post-harvest waste fell 15%, market-grade fruit jumped from 70% to 88%, and the farm's turnover nearly doubled. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Drone-Delivered Vaccines Reached 3.9 Million Nigerian Children Who Missed Routine Shots
item.description: Cross River State's zero-dose project used Zipline drones and 160 field teams across nine local government areas to reach children in riverine and mountainous areas where roads made conventional delivery nearly impossible. Zipline's Africa CEO says zero-dose prevalence fell 36% in Cross River and 42% in Bayelsa. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: An AI Fall-Prevention System Gave a Senior Living Community Its First Fall-Free Month
item.description: United Zion Retirement Community rejected cameras, which residents saw as a dignity risk, and instead used Helpany's radar-based AI that learns each resident's baseline and flags fall risk before it strikes. Falls dropped 70% and the community logged its first-ever month without a single fall. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Two New Pharmacy Robots Dispense Medicine Four Times Faster Than a Person at NHS Hospitals
item.description: Colchester and Ipswich hospitals have upgraded their pharmacy teams with robots that pick and dispense medication at super speed while checking expiry dates on every packet. Every item is still checked by a human eye before it reaches a patient, freeing staff to process more prescriptions safely. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: AI Cut a Chinese City's District Heating Energy Waste by Over 10%
item.description: In Changsha, a district heating operator serving 60,000 people ran an AI system through a full heating season to forecast demand and catch faults before they wasted energy. Electricity consumption fell by more than 10% and the heat needed dropped 7%, while residents stayed warm. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Kentucky Farmer Planted 900 Acres of Corn Without Anyone in the Tractor Cab
item.description: Quint Pottinger fitted a $70,000 Sabanto autonomy kit to a John Deere 6130E and planted 900 acres of corn autonomously this spring, after a 500-acre autonomous wheat planting last fall. He has since sold two large planters, two big tractors and a combine, returning nearly $500,000 in equipment capital to his eighth-generation farm. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: One Blood Test Caught 6.5 Times More Cancers in the Largest US Trial of Its Kind
item.description: In the largest interventional multi-cancer early detection trial in North America, 35,878 adults took GRAIL's Galleri blood test alongside standard screening, and cancer detection rose 6.5-fold. Seventy percent of the newly found cancers have no recommended screening at all, and one participant, Franklin Weingarten, 88, is cancer-free today after the test caught his bile duct cancer early. (Kudos level 3: Legend.)

item.title: An AI Recycling Robot Started Sorting Sarasota's Waste at 60 Picks a Minute
item.description: A Glacier AI-powered robot joined the Circular Services plant in Sarasota, pulling aluminum cans and HDPE plastics off a line that processes 50 tons of recycling an hour. Glacier's robots already sort recycling for about 1 in 10 Americans, keeping valuable commodities out of landfills and easing the grind of line work. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: A 15-Minute Blood Test and AI Helped a Hospital Rethink Sepsis Care
item.description: Tampa General Hospital paired its Palantir-built Sepsis Hub with MeMed's 15-minute blood test that reads the immune response to tell bacterial infections from viral ones. In an 893-patient study, 26% more patients were safely reclassified as unlikely to have sepsis, cefepime use fell by a third, hospitalizations dropped 13%, and savings reached about $179,000 per 100 patients. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: An Automated Plant in Italy Began Turning 19,200 Tonnes of Textile Waste Back Into Spinning Fiber
item.description: IGERS inaugurated a new automated textile recycling plant near Novara that uses near-infrared optical sorters to identify pure cotton and wool fractions, then mechanically regenerates them into flakes and opened fibers for the spinning industry. The 8 million euro facility tracks every material stream digitally from buffering to final output. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: Google's Medical AI Interviewed Real Patients in a First-of-Its-Kind Lancet Study
item.description: In the first prospective real-world study of its kind, published in The Lancet, 98 patients at a Boston primary care clinic talked through their symptoms with Google's AMIE chatbot before urgent appointments, with a physician watching every chat. No conversation needed a safety stop, the AI's differential matched the final diagnosis 90% of the time, and doctors said its summaries helped them prepare in three-quarters of cases. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: One in Five Americans Has Ridden in a Robotaxi, and 83% Say the Ride Changed Their Mind
item.description: A Cox Automotive survey found about one in five Americans has now ridden in a driverless car, and among those riders 83% said their perception of autonomous vehicles improved. Sam Abuelsamid of Telemetry notes riders tend to walk away with a much better impression once they actually experience the technology. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: An AI Coaching App Helped Hypertension Patients Take Control of Their Blood Pressure
item.description: In a Rush University Medical Center study published in the Journal of General Internal Medicine, 425 patients added the free Nuna app, with its AI health coach and gamified reminders, to their hypertension care. Systolic blood pressure fell 13.6 mm Hg among users with uncontrolled stage 2 hypertension versus 9.0 among controls, and one in five participants brought their high blood pressure under control early in the study. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: An AI Reading Tutor Nearly Quadrupled Struggling Readers' Odds of Catching Up
item.description: Perry Township Schools in Indiana deployed the Project Read AI tutor, which listens to young children read aloud and gives sound-by-sound feedback, across four schools. Among the 520 students who started the year below benchmark, a student using the tutor 30 minutes a week had roughly a 68% chance of catching up, nearly four times the odds of one barely using it. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: An AI That Reads Breast MRIs to Predict Cancer Recurrence Won FDA Clearance
item.description: SimBioSys won FDA 510(k) clearance for TumorSight Risk, the first AI tool that estimates breast cancer recurrence risk from routine MRI scans, validated on 2,129 patients across multiple institutions. It needs no extra procedures or hardware, giving oncologists personalized five- and ten-year risk scores before surgery. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: The First Treatment for Schizophrenia's Negative Symptoms Is a Smartphone App
item.description: Click Therapeutics' Motivista became the first FDA-authorized treatment for the negative symptoms of schizophrenia, delivered as a 16-week smartphone program alongside standard care. In its phase 3 trial, patients improved 62 percent more than those using a control app. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A One-Step Rapid Syphilis Test Catches the Infection Earlier
item.description: Penn State researchers built a one-step rapid syphilis test that detects the disease sooner by swapping gold nanoparticles for layered silver-and-gold ones, producing test lines up to 46 percent stronger. Catching syphilis earlier means faster treatment and fewer clinic visits. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Tongue-Controlled Exoskeleton Restored Hand Use After Spinal Cord Injury
item.description: Researchers in Denmark and the Netherlands showed that five people with cervical spinal cord injuries could steer a soft hand exoskeleton with their tongues, restoring grasping for daily tasks like holding a bottle or a toothbrush. Participants reported high task success with low discomfort and fatigue. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Smart Sensors Are Watching Over 600 Elderly People Living Alone in Hefei
item.description: In Hefei, China, door sensors and smoke detectors in the homes of more than 600 elderly residents now alert community workers when no activity is detected for 24 hours or an alarm trips. Around a dozen alerts a day get follow-up through a three-tier response of family, community workers and officials. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Solar Desalination Box Is Keeping a Remote Aboriginal School Flowing
item.description: Murdoch University's solar-powered desalination unit, small enough to fit inside a shipping container, is now supplying a remote Aboriginal boarding school that the water grid cannot reach. It has delivered more than 7.5 megalitres of freshwater, with students helping keep the operating logs. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Water Droplets Wired Into Brain-Like Networks Compute With Ions, Not Electrons
item.description: Penn State engineers built soft networks of water droplets that process information like brain tissue, using ions instead of electrons at a far lower energy cost. In early tests, connected droplet networks cut prediction error by nearly half compared with isolated ones. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: The First Engineered Geothermal Plant Is Now Selling Power to the Grid
item.description: Fervo Energy's Cape Station in Utah became the first greenfield enhanced geothermal project anywhere to synchronize to the grid and enter commercial operation, with its first 33-megawatt block now earning revenue. A second 400-megawatt phase is already under construction. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Free All-Terrain Wheelchairs Opened Utah's National Park Trails to Everyone
item.description: The National Park Service is now offering free all-terrain wheelchairs at Zion, Bryce, Canyonlands, Arches and Capitol Reef, opening unpaved trails to visitors with limited mobility. The balloon-tired chairs handle sand, rocks and ledges on a first-come, first-served basis. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Five Deaf Schoolgirls Built an AI App for Menstrual Health and Reached a Global Final
item.description: Five deaf schoolgirls from Abuja, Nigeria, became global finalists at the 2026 Technovation Girls World Summit with Saving Pad, an AI-powered app that maps nearby sanitary pad banks and tracks supplies. They have already piloted it across three special schools, with plans to expand nationwide. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Battery Waste Became Pouch Cells That Last Nearly Twice as Long
item.description: Researchers at Worcester Polytechnic Institute turned mixed battery waste into upgraded cathodes and graphite anodes, then built full pouch cells from nothing but the upcycled materials. The cells held 70% of their capacity after 2,590 cycles, nearly double the life of cells made with commercial materials, in research published in Advanced Energy Materials. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: The World's First Purpose-Built Offshore Carbon Storage Platform Is Installed
item.description: Eni CCUS Holding installed the Douglas platform in Liverpool Bay, the first offshore platform built specifically for carbon capture and storage serving industrial decarbonization. As the hub of the HyNet cluster, it will funnel CO2 captured from factories across North West England and North Wales into depleted gas reservoirs for permanent storage. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: 47 Randomized Trials Find AI Tools Lift Student Achievement
item.description: Researchers pooled 47 randomized controlled trials and found AI interventions raised academic achievement with a medium-to-large effect, roughly the size of some of the best conventional teaching programs. Gains leveled off after about 23 hours of use, a handy guide for schools deploying the tech thoughtfully. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: FDA Clears an AI That Cuts False Alarms From Implantable Heart Monitors
item.description: The FDA granted 510(k) clearance to Implicity's cloud-based AI analyzer, a manufacturer-agnostic second layer that re-checks alerts from implantable cardiac monitors made by Abbott, Biotronik, Boston Scientific and Medtronic. Published research shows it cut false-positive episodes by up to 76% while keeping high sensitivity for real events, easing the review burden on cardiac care teams. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Automated Insulin Delivery Wins FDA Clearance for Type 2 Diabetes
item.description: Sequel Med Tech won FDA clearance to extend its twiist automated insulin delivery system to adults with type 2 diabetes, a population the company estimates at 5.5 million insulin users in the US. The pharmacy-dispensed pump pairs with popular continuous glucose monitors and continuously adjusts basal insulin using the Tidepool Loop algorithm. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Nigerian Bionic Arm Matched to Black Skin Tones Lands on TIME's Best Inventions List
item.description: The Ubokobong Bionic Arm pairs muscle-controlled movement with a hyper-realistic look designed for Black amputees, and it is already in use by clients in 56 countries. It grew from two brothers' own experience after one lost his fingers in a fireworks accident and could not find a prosthetic that matched his skin tone. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Thought-Controlled Bionic Arm Moved Into Its First Real Home
item.description: Alexander 'Avi' Davidson is the first person to use the University of Utah's nerve-interfaced bionic arm unsupervised at home, steering the hand with his thoughts and feeling touch through it. Within days he was writing, playing cards, making a sandwich, and holding his wife's hand while feeling the pressure back. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: In England, 1,000 Companion Robots Are Helping Older People Live Independently
item.description: Vera Gadsdon, 74, is one of more than 1,000 people across England now using Cera's Genie companion robots, which remind residents to eat, drink, and take medication while keeping them company between carer visits. Trials showed a 96% success rate in prompting the right medication at the right time. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Tactile Tablet Lets Blind Fans Feel Live Sports Action
item.description: OneCourt's tablet turns real-time player and ball tracking data into vibrations, so blind and low-vision fans can follow the game with their fingertips. Named to TIME's 2026 Best Inventions list, it was used at Super Bowl 60, where fans felt the ball's movement as it happened. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Wallpaper That Generates Electricity From Room Humidity Powered a Keyboard
item.description: Binghamton University engineers built wallpaper from 1,596 tiny moisture-electric generators that turn indoor humidity into a steady current, enough to power a wireless keyboard. The paper also evens out room humidity as it works, and the team designed it to be printable for mass production. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Surgical Robot That Lets Surgeons Feel Tissue Operated in a UK First
item.description: Surgeons at St Thomas' Hospital in London used new Force Feedback instruments on a da Vinci 5 robot for the first time in the UK, letting them feel tissue resistance through the console controls. The first patient, 57-year-old Nicholas Kokkinos, was up and moving a day after his hernia repair with barely noticeable incision pain. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: The FDA Approved the First Heart Valve That Grows With Children
item.description: The FDA approved Edwards Lifesciences' Autus valve on October 1, the first heart valve designed to expand as a child grows, from 13 mm up to adult size via a balloon catheter. In a 62-patient trial every child was free of device complications at 30 days, and the polymer leaflets could spare kids from repeat open-heart surgeries. (Kudos level 3: Legend.)

item.title: Europe Sold a Record 600,000 EVs in September
item.description: Europeans bought nearly 600,000 electric vehicles in September, a monthly record up 39% from a year earlier, with the UK, France, Spain, Portugal and Finland all posting their best months ever. Battery electrics did the heavy lifting, jumping 50% year over year. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: New England's Wind Power Hit Record After Record This Fall
item.description: Wind turbines in New England generated 68% more electricity in the first nine months of 2026 than the same period last year, with September output more than doubling year over year. Nine months of wind power already beat all of 2025's total. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Smart Ring Won FDA Clearance to Track Blood Pressure Without a Cuff
item.description: The FDA cleared Happy Health's smart ring for continuous blood pressure monitoring with no cuff and no calibration, validated against arterial-line measurements with under 1 mmHg mean error. It builds on the ring's existing clearance for at-home sleep apnea diagnosis. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: An AI Tool That Helps Diagnose Autism in Toddlers Won FDA Clearance
item.description: The FDA cleared Argus Cognitive's Neurora, software that measures over 100 vocal, facial and gaze biometrics from a standard behavioral assessment to support autism diagnosis in children as young as 18 months. With autism affecting 1 in 31 US children and median diagnosis near age 4, earlier objective evidence could get kids help sooner. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Blind Veterans Ran a 10-Miler With AI Glasses, and Now Every Blind Veteran Gets a Pair Free
item.description: Eight runners including blind Army veterans Roosevelt Morring, Rob Sanchas and Shawntina Gibson finished the Army Ten-Miler in heavy rain wearing Meta AI glasses that described the world around them. Meta committed to giving free Ray-Ban Meta AI glasses to every blind veteran in America, more than 130,000 people. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Water-Based Battery Glue Could Make Lithium Batteries Easier to Recycle
item.description: UC San Diego engineers created a fluorine-free battery binder from two cheap polymers linked with citric acid, replacing toxic solvents with plain water. Batteries built with it matched conventional performance, held capacity longer, and the electrodes could be recycled by simply soaking them in water. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A New Catalyst Gave Rechargeable Zinc-Air Batteries 300 Hours of Runtime
item.description: Chemists at TU Darmstadt built a nickel-iron-carbon catalyst that let rechargeable zinc-air batteries survive 500 charge cycles. Since zinc-air can theoretically store five times the energy of lithium-ion, the advance revives a chemistry long stuck as single-use. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Wood Waste Made Lithium Batteries Safer and 60% Longer-Lasting
item.description: Michigan State engineers turned lignin, a cheap wood waste from paper mills, into a battery separator that withstands heat three times better than plastic. Batteries using it lasted 60% longer in testing, a step toward taming lithium-ion fire risk. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: A Hornbill Made History With the World's First Double 3D-Printed Beak
item.description: A young southern ground hornbill at Amsterdam's Artis Zoo broke both his upper and lower beak, leaving him unable to eat or preen. Vets at Utrecht University fitted him with two custom 3D-printed titanium prostheses, and he was picking up food with his new beak the very next morning. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: J&J's OTTAVA Becomes the First Table-Integrated Surgical Robot to Win FDA Authorization
item.description: After an 11-year development journey, Johnson & Johnson's OTTAVA system earned FDA market authorization for 10 general surgery procedures including gastric bypass. The design stows its robotic arms inside the operating table itself, freeing up space around the patient and tightening surgical workflows. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A New Wireless Power System Keeps Stretchy Medical Implants Running in a Moving Body
item.description: South Korean researchers built a stretchable liquid-metal receiver that keeps implants powered even as the body twists and deforms. In animal tests it ran a soft cardiac pacemaker reliably, a step toward implants that conform to living tissue without wires. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Gene Therapy Gave Deaf Children Their Hearing Back.
item.description: A one-time gene therapy infusion restored meaningful hearing in 9 of 12 children with profound inherited deafness, no implants required. One three-year-old went from near-total deafness to hearing in the normal range within weeks. (Kudos level 3: Legend.)

item.title: America Passed 80,000 Public Fast-Charging Ports
item.description: America passed 80,000 public fast-charging ports after 4,106 were added in a single quarter, 73% of new ports at 250 kW or more, with a record 17.6 million charging sessions in July. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Tanzania Brought School to 751 Children With Disabilities
item.description: Tanzania's new inclusive education strategy brought schooling to 751 children with disabilities through home- and hospital-based learning, 440 laptops and tablets, over 522,000 Braille and large-print books, and compulsory sign-language training for student teachers. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Wearable Robot Helped ALS Patients Walk Farther
item.description: A Toho University study found 30 ALS patients walked nearly 12 meters farther in a two-minute test after training with the Hybrid Assistive Limb, a wearable robot that reads faint muscle signals to amplify the wearer's own intended movement, while quality of life stayed stable. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: CRISPR Chip Names the Bacteria Behind Hard-to-Diagnose Lung Infections in Hours, Not Weeks
item.description: Tulane and UNC researchers built CANDI, a CRISPR microfluidic chip that identifies 15 nontuberculous mycobacteria species from patient samples in about 3.5 hours, work that culture tests need four to six weeks to do. In 230 clinical samples it matched the right species 97.3% of the time, which means patients can start the right treatment far sooner. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Waymo Robotaxis Have Prevented an Estimated 841 Injury Crashes
item.description: Across 271 million rider-only miles through June 2026, Waymo reports 95% fewer serious-injury crashes and 82% fewer injury crashes than human benchmarks, adding up to an estimated 841 injury crashes that never happened. Cyclist and pedestrian injury crashes fell even further, down 86% and 93%. (Kudos level 3: Legend.)

item.title: Self-Balancing Exoskeleton Eve Gets FDA Clearance to Walk People Home
item.description: Wandercraft's Eve is the first self-balancing personal exoskeleton cleared by the FDA, letting people with spinal cord injuries stand and walk at home with no crutches or walker. In its clearance study, 87.5% of users completed everyday tasks like opening doors and cooking, and US sales have begun. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: One Robot Printer and a Crew of Three Built Europe's Largest 3D-Printed Housing Project
item.description: At Skovsporet in Holstebro, Denmark, a single COBOD BOD3 printer and a three-person crew printed 36 student apartments across six buildings, finishing one six-apartment building in five working days. The homes came in within Denmark's affordable-housing budget cap, kept 90% of the site's trees, and have already welcomed their first residents. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Google's Retinal AI Has Now Screened More Than a Million Patients for Diabetic Eye Disease
item.description: ARDA, Google's diabetic retinopathy screening AI, has passed one million patients screened through partner clinics at Aravind Eye Care in India, Rajavithi Hospital in Thailand and Lions Outback Vision in Australia. The screenings run at no cost to patients, with a goal of six million across India and Thailand within ten years. (Kudos level 3: Legend.)

item.title: Solar Tablets Bring Adaptive Lessons to 57,000 Tanzanian Primary Schoolers
item.description: MsingiTEK has put solar-powered adaptive-learning tablets into 250 public primary schools across five Tanzanian regions, reaching more than 57,000 children in grades 1 to 3. Teachers report better attendance and stronger reading, writing and counting, and the programme is on its way to 500 schools and 120,000 students. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Suitcase Robot Guides Visually Impaired Walkers Through Tokyo
item.description: A suitcase-shaped AI robot developed by Japan's Miraikan science museum is guiding visually impaired people through Tokyo's Toranomon Hills in a month-long public trial, using cameras and sensors to steer around obstacles. Its built-in chatbot can also answer questions about shops and routes along the way. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Record Quarter for US Clean Power as 17.1 GW Came Online
item.description: 164 utility-scale clean energy projects came online in the US in a single quarter, up 45% on the year, pushing total clean capacity to about 388 gigawatts. The quarter included SunZia, the largest land-based wind project in American history. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: An Autonomous AI Triaged Skin Cancer Referrals Across Two UK Hospitals
item.description: A CE-marked AI autonomously discharged 25 to 31% of urgent suspected skin cancer referrals across two UK hospitals, 8,391 patients, saving 2,851 clinician hours. The first large-scale real-world autonomous AI deployment in a cancer pathway. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: GM Started Shipping EVs With Fully Recycled Battery Cells
item.description: GM's closed-loop pilot turned 80 end-of-life battery packs into cathode material with 100% recycled nickel, cobalt, and manganese, certified to match virgin material, and the first EVs carrying those cells are now shipping to customers. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Two Humanoid Robots Joined a Live Packaging Line in Korea
item.description: CJ Logistics put two dual-arm humanoids to work stuffing cushioning into boxes at a fulfillment center, the first live logistics humanoid deployment in South Korea. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: AI Eye Screening in Primary Care Halved the Cost of Catching Diabetic Retinopathy
item.description: Autonomous AI eye screening in a Canadian primary-care clinic completed 93.6% of exams on the spot and cut the cost per diagnosed case of diabetic retinopathy roughly in half. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: A Smartphone App Guided Blind Users 13% Faster With 41% Fewer Bumps
item.description: Harvard's Mobilio smartphone app, with pedestrian-view AI and personalized audio cues, guided 14 blind and low-vision participants 13% faster with 41% fewer bumps, at reliability comparable to a human guide. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Double Neural Bypass Rewired a Paralyzed Man's Nervous System.
item.description: Keith Thomas, completely paralyzed since 2020, regained hand movement and wrist sensation through brain implants paired with AI-decoded stimulation. Remarkably, the gains persisted more than two years after stimulation stopped. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Prosthetic Hand That Learns Each Amputee's Unique Muscle Signals
item.description: A 3D-scanned, 3D-printed sleeve with magnetic sensors plus individualized AI decoded 19 hand gestures in real time for ten participants, including three amputees. It stayed accurate after 7,500 force cycles. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A 5.5-Pound Hip Exoskeleton Cut Stroke Survivors' Walking Effort by 18%
item.description: A portable hip exoskeleton offloaded about 30% of hip work for stroke survivors with hemiparesis, cutting walking effort 18%. Some gait gains persisted after the device came off. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Trimming a Rice Gene Lifted Yields 25% and Drought Tolerance
item.description: Chicago scientists trimmed a section of rice's own ALKBH9 and ALKBH10 genes, no foreign DNA, and boosted harvests 20 to 25% with better drought and heat tolerance. Published in Nature Genetics. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: The World Installed a Record 664 GW of Solar in 2025.
item.description: The world installed a record 664 gigawatts of solar in 2025, pushing the global fleet past 3 terawatts, triple its size four years ago. Solar now supplies about 9% of all electricity generated on Earth. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Resistance Robot Taught Kids With SMA to Stand Up on Their Own
item.description: A 2.1-pound knee robot that resists rather than assists movement helped six children with spinal muscular atrophy gain 130% quadriceps strength. All of them can now rise from a chair unassisted. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Humanoid Robot Helped Build 30,000 BMWs Over an 11-Month Run
item.description: A Figure 02 humanoid worked 10-hour shifts at BMW's Spartanburg plant inserting sheet-metal parts for welding at better than 99% accuracy per shift, helping build 30,000 cars over an 11-month run. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: AI Thermal Imaging and Drones Now Guard Kenya's Wildlife Parks
item.description: The Kenya Wildlife Service embedded AI thermal imaging, drones, and EarthRanger into daily ranger operations, with real-time poacher alerts across its parks. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: Solar Panels Over California Canals Cut Evaporation by Up to 70%
item.description: Project Nexus, a 1.6 MW pilot covering Turlock Irrigation District canals with solar panels, measured evaporation reductions of 50 to 70% and 85% less algae growth over a full irrigation season, while the water below kept the panels cooler and more productive. Covering California's canal network could one day save an estimated 63 billion gallons a year. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: The World Installed a Record 112 GW of Grid Batteries in 2025.
item.description: Grid battery installations jumped 48% to a record 112 gigawatts in 2025, ten times the 2021 level, as lithium-ion prices kept falling. Storage is finally catching up with the solar boom. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: One in Four Cars Sold Worldwide Was Electric in 2025.
item.description: More than 20 million electric cars sold in 2025, a full quarter of all cars sold worldwide and a first-ever milestone. Emerging markets doubled their sales in a single year. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: AI Scribes Gave Doctors 16 Minutes Back Per Patient Visit
item.description: A JAMA multisite study across five academic centers found ambient AI scribes cut clinician documentation by 16 minutes per patient visit in real clinics, a modest but genuine productivity gain. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: Green Hydrogen Unlocked Low-Grade Ore for Climate-Neutral Steel
item.description: A Namibian pilot converted 80 tonnes of low-grade iron ore into direct-reduced iron using green hydrogen, unlocking ore grades conventional green-steel routes cannot touch. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: An Open AI Model for Protein Structures Released Its Full Training Stack
item.description: OpenFold3 released its training datasets, weights, and code under permissive licenses: an open protein-structure AI competitive with AlphaFold3. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Baby Got the World's First Personalized CRISPR Therapy. A Year Later, He's Walking and Talking.
item.description: KJ Muldoon was born with a fatal metabolic disorder and no treatment options. Six months later a bespoke CRISPR edit built for his exact mutation had him walking, talking, and eating protein safely, and his case pushed the FDA to create a faster path for personalized therapies. (Kudos level 3: Legend.)

item.title: Closed-Loop Insulin Pumps Beat Sensor Pumps Across 27 Trials
item.description: A meta-analysis of 27 randomized trials with over 1,000 participants found hybrid closed-loop insulin pumps raised time in range 8.8 points over sensor-augmented pumps, supporting NHS England's expansion plan. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Orange County's Water Recycler Passed Half a Trillion Gallons
item.description: Orange County's Groundwater Replenishment System, the world's largest advanced purification plant for potable reuse, passed half a trillion gallons over 18 years, now recycling 100% of reclaimable flows for up to 2.5 million people. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Copper Smelter Now Heats Thousands of Hamburg Homes
item.description: Waste heat from the Aurubis copper smelter now travels 3.7 km into Hamburg's district heating network, warming thousands of homes and saving up to 120,000 tonnes of CO2 a year. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: China Approved the World's First Commercial Brain Implant for Paralysis.
item.description: China approved the first brain implant for commercial use in paralysis, with Neuracle's NEO restoring hand movement. A paralyzed hand moving again is not a gadget; it is independence, returned. (Kudos level 3: Legend.)

item.title: A Malaria Vaccine Reached a Refugee Camp. Child Deaths Fell by Half.
item.description: MSF completed the first full malaria vaccine campaign ever run in a refugee camp, fully vaccinating 2,100 young children in Ethiopia's Kule camp. In the months after, the camp hospital recorded roughly half as many child malaria deaths as the year before. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Brain Implant Let a Paralyzed Man Drive a Wheelchair and Command a Robot Dog
item.description: A man paralyzed since 2022 steers a smart wheelchair outdoors, sends a robot dog on errands, and does paid remote computer work, all through a fully implanted wireless brain-computer interface with under 100ms latency. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: An AI Bionic Hand That Grasps Without Making Amputees Think
item.description: Proximity and pressure sensing plus a neural net let a commercial bionic hand auto-position its fingers, so four amputees got a more secure grip with far less mental effort. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: India Hit 50% Non-Fossil Power Capacity Five Years Early
item.description: India crossed 50% non-fossil power capacity in June 2025, five years ahead of its Paris target, after adding a record 48 to 50 gigawatts of renewables in a single year. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Hospital-Level Care Came Home to Rural America
item.description: A 161-patient randomized trial of hospital-level care at home: wireless chest-sticker telemetry, fanny-pack IV pumps, handheld lab meters. Costs 27% lower with early transfer, patients walked 700 more steps a day, satisfaction 88 versus 46. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: 2Africa, the Longest Subsea Cable Ever Built, Is Complete
item.description: 2Africa, the longest subsea cable ever built at 45,000 km around the continent, is complete. The hard part now is the middle and last mile getting that capacity to people. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Perovskite Solar Cells Hit a Record 27.2% Efficiency.
item.description: Researchers set a new 27.2% efficiency record for perovskite solar cells with a simple potassium additive that also made the cells far more durable. Cheap, high-efficiency panels just got meaningfully closer. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: Solar-Powered Links Brought 10,000 Rural Kenyans Online for School
item.description: Kenya's education network wired 20 rural institutions through university hubs with solar backup, bringing 10,000 rural Kenyans online for school. One college's 100 idle donated computers became a working lab. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Gene Therapy Cured 95% of Children Born Without an Immune System.
item.description: In the largest and longest-tracked cohort of its kind, 59 of 62 children born with ADA-SCID were cured by lentiviral gene therapy, with 100% survival over seven and a half years. Kids who once would not have lived past two are now in school and playing sports. (Kudos level 3: Legend.)

item.title: A Rice-Grain Chip Let Blind Patients Read Again.
item.description: A rice-grain-sized retinal implant paired with AR glasses restored reading vision in 84% of patients with untreatable macular degeneration. On average they gained five lines on the vision chart. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: The World's First Pressure-Geothermal Storage Plant Built in Texas
item.description: Sage Geosystems built the world's first pressure-geothermal storage plant in Texas in 12 months: engineered underground fractures store energy at 70 to 75% round-trip efficiency with up to 17 hours of discharge. It connected to the grid in December 2025. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Switzerland Released Apertus, a Fully Open Multilingual AI Model
item.description: EPFL, ETH Zurich and CSCS released Apertus, a multilingual AI model trained on public infrastructure with weights, data, and training recipes all public under Apache 2.0. AI for the public good, not a commercial launch. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Sensors on Power Lines Unlocked Nearly 50% More Grid Capacity in Minnesota
item.description: Great River Energy's dynamic line rating deployment, the largest in the US by sensor count, found 48.92% more capacity on a pilot transmission line, going from pilot to full deployment in under nine months. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Bionic Knee That Feels Like Part of Your Body.
item.description: MIT built a prosthetic knee anchored to bone and wired into the nervous system, and the first two amputees to receive it walked faster, climbed stairs, and said it felt like part of themselves. Published in Science. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Lab-Grown Islet Cells Freed 10 of 12 Diabetics From Insulin.
item.description: A single infusion of lab-grown islet cells left 10 of 12 adults with severe type 1 diabetes fully insulin-independent a year later. All twelve were free of dangerous low-blood-sugar episodes, a scalable alternative to donor transplants. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Beach-Cleaning Robot Joined the Great Lakes Cleanup.
item.description: Canada's first BeBot, a remote-controlled beach-cleaning robot, started work on Ontario's Great Lakes shores in summer 2025. It sieves microplastics from sand at up to 3,000 square meters per hour. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: The World's Largest Reverse-Osmosis Desalination Plant Certified
item.description: Saudi Arabia's Al Khobar RO2 was certified the world's largest reverse-osmosis desalination plant at 670,852 cubic meters a day. Its sister plant set the world record for the lowest RO energy use. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: AI Tutoring Lifted Nigerian Students' English Scores.
item.description: A World Bank trial gave Nigerian students GPT-4-powered after-school tutoring and watched English scores rise by 0.31 standard deviations, with the biggest gains for girls. At $48 per student, it ranks among the most cost-effective education interventions ever measured. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Plant That Turns Captured CO2 Into Limestone Opened in Norfolk
item.description: Mission Zero's electrochemical plant in Norfolk pulls 250 tonnes of CO2 a year from the air and turns it into carbon-negative limestone for bricks and concrete: the world's first fully integrated direct-air-capture-to-building-materials plant, operating commercially. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Cyborg Cockroaches Joined a Real Earthquake Rescue.
item.description: After the March 2025 Myanmar earthquake, Singapore's rescue team deployed ten camera-equipped cyborg cockroaches into rubble too tight for humans or dogs. A world first for the technology, in a real disaster. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Sunlight-and-Seawater Device Makes Green Hydrogen and Drinking Water
item.description: A low-cost device that needs only sunlight and seawater to produce green hydrogen and clean drinking water, with no grid power required. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: A Brain Implant Steered a Robotic Arm for Seven Months Without Recalibration
item.description: UCSF researchers showed a paralyzed man could control a robotic arm for reaching and grasping for a record seven months, because the AI adapted to small day-to-day shifts in brain activity. Previous implants typically needed recalibration within days. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Prosthetic Liner You Adjust From Your Phone
item.description: A silicone prosthetic liner with pressurized channels lets amputees adjust the fit in real time from a smartphone. Six trial users reported far fewer frustrating fits, meaning fewer blisters, sores, and returns to the wheelchair. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: A Bone-Anchored Implant Got an Amputee Walking Again After a Decade
item.description: After a decade of failed socket prostheses, a titanium implant anchored directly into the patient's femur got him walking unaided. He even senses the ground through the bone itself. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Prosthetic Hand That Restores Touch and Cut Phantom Pain by 90%
item.description: Spinal and peripheral nerve stimulation let an amputee distinguish object sizes by touch through a prosthesis, with no training. Phantom limb pain fell 90%. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Rescue Robot Pulled Tourists From Rough Water in Hainan
item.description: A U-shaped water rescue robot pulled struggling tourists from the surf in Hainan during its first Spring Festival deployment. It is now in service in Fujian and Guangdong too. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: A Brain Implant Decoded Finger Movements to Fly a Drone
item.description: A quadriplegic patient steered a virtual drone through obstacle courses using only decoded finger movements from his motor cortex. Three independent finger groups, read straight from the brain (Nature Medicine). (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Dual-Arm Robot Picks Apples at Near-Human Speed
item.description: A dual-arm harvester built with Michigan State picks an apple every three seconds using AI vision, at near-human speed. The USDA positions it as a commercially viable answer to orchard labor costs. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Stem Cells Reversed Type 1 Diabetes in a Woman.
item.description: A reprogrammed stem cell transplant reversed Type 1 diabetes in a woman, reported in Nature. A milestone for a disease once thought irreversible. (Kudos level 3: Legend.)

item.title: Blue Origin Made Solar Cells From Moon Dust.
item.description: Blue Origin figured out how to make solar cells from Moon dust. With Blue Alchemist, the lunar surface could power its own future. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Gene Editing Might Cure HIV. The First Trial Results Are In.
item.description: A startup's CRISPR approach to curing HIV has reported its first trial results. An old dream of medicine is being tested in the real world. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: AI and Automation Are Collapsing the Drug Discovery Timeline.
item.description: AI and automation are shrinking the drug discovery timeline, finding the right drug for the right patient faster. Speed that saves lives. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: CRISPR's Next Act: Fighting Climate Change and Feeding the World.
item.description: The CRISPR pioneers are aiming gene editing at climate change and world hunger. After medicine, the next act is the planet itself. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Exoskeleton Technology Could Redefine Disability.
item.description: Exoskeleton technology is poised to redefine disability, making wheelchairs optional rather than inevitable. Standing, walking, and meeting the world at eye level again: that is what progress feels like. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Paralyzed With a Severed Spinal Cord, He Walks Again.
item.description: With a severed spinal cord, he walked again after an implant bridged his injury. Medicine just did the miraculous. (Kudos level 3: Legend.)

item.title: A New Drug Delays Type 1 Diabetes in Kids.
item.description: A new drug can delay type 1 diabetes in kids, buying them a full, normal childhood. Sometimes the best gift is more time. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: The Hubble Is Falling. SpaceX Might Give It a Lift.
item.description: The Hubble is falling, and SpaceX plus a billionaire backer are exploring a mission to lift it back up. Even our greatest telescopes deserve a second act. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: The Living Lights That Could Cut Our Energy Use.
item.description: Scientists are exploring bioluminescence, nature's own glow, as a way to light cities and cut energy use. Streets lit by living light: quieter, softer, and gentler on the planet. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Can Nuclear Fusion Put the Brakes on Climate Change?
item.description: The New Yorker examined whether nuclear fusion could help slow climate change, laying out the science and the stakes. The dream of clean, near-limitless energy is still alive, and still worth chasing. (Kudos level 3: Legend.)

item.title: The Material That "Learns" Like a Sea Slug.
item.description: Nickel oxide, a humble material, showed learning behaviors like a sea slug's: habituation and sensitization in its electrical responses. Matter that learns could one day become AI hardware that sips power instead of gulping it. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: He Typed 90 Characters a Minute Using Only His Thoughts.
item.description: A paralyzed man typed 90 characters a minute just by imagining handwriting, decoded by a Stanford brain implant. His thoughts became words at smartphone speed: communication, restored. (Kudos level 3: Legend.)

item.title: Alphabet's Wing Drones Hit 100,000 Deliveries.
item.description: Alphabet's Wing drones crossed 100,000 deliveries, proof that the quiet work of delivery drones is paying off. Slowly, then suddenly. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: Overnight Success Takes Decades: The mRNA Story.
item.description: The mRNA miracle was decades in the making, built on years of patient, unglamorous work. Overnight success takes decades. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: The Battery Made of Rust That Stores Power for 100 Hours.
item.description: Form Energy's iron-air battery stores power for 100 hours at a tenth of lithium's cost, using rust. The humble battery just got heroic. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Brain Implant Turned a Paralyzed Man's Thoughts Into Words.
item.description: A brain implant turned a paralyzed man's thoughts directly into words, giving him back his voice. Communication, restored from within. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: An mRNA Vaccine Fully Immunized Mice Against Malaria.
item.description: An mRNA vaccine fully protected mice against malaria in trials. The same platform that fought COVID is now taking aim at one of humanity's oldest killers. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: The Malaria Vaccine That Beat Expectations at 77% Efficacy.
item.description: A malaria vaccine beat expectations with 77% efficacy, the first to clear the WHO's 75% bar, and it costs about $2 a dose. A landmark win against a global killer. (Kudos level 3: Legend.)

item.title: The FDA Approved VR Movies as a Treatment for Lazy Eye.
item.description: The FDA approved VR movies as real therapy for kids' lazy eye. Amblyopia treatment just became movie night. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Your Cough Has a Sound. AI Can Hear Disease in It.
item.description: AI can hear disease in a cough, turning a smartphone into a respiratory diagnostic tool. A simple sound check could catch illness early. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Drones Flew Blood to a Remote Hospital in 18 Minutes.
item.description: In Uttarakhand, drones delivered blood to a remote hospital in just 18 minutes, skipping terrain that once meant hours of travel. A beautiful leapfrog moment, where the sky becomes the fastest road to care. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: The CAD Program for Designing Organisms From Scratch.
item.description: GP-write's genome CAD program lets scientists design organisms the way engineers design circuits, on a screen, before they are built. Biology is getting the drafting tools that made software and chips scale. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: An AI App Is Reading Chest X-Rays for TB in Rural India.
item.description: Qure.ai's AI reads chest X-rays for tuberculosis in rural India, bringing expert diagnosis where doctors are scarce. Healthcare capacity, multiplied by software. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: The World's Best Hope for Enough Covid Vaccine.
item.description: The Serum Institute's massive manufacturing scale-up became the world's best hope for enough vaccine. Scale, it turns out, is a superpower. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Europe Approved the First Artificial Heart for Sale.
item.description: Europe approved Carmat's artificial heart for sale, a device born from aerospace engineering. A heart built like a spacecraft, now pumping blood in real chests: medicine borrowing from the stars. (Kudos level 3: Legend.)

item.title: A Robotic Teddy Bear Is Making Hospitalized Kids Feel Better.
item.description: MIT's Huggable, a robotic teddy bear, helped more than 50 hospitalized kids feel better in a Pediatrics study. Sometimes the best medicine is a warm, patient friend. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Gene Therapies for Rare Diseases Are Here.
item.description: One-shot gene therapies for rare diseases have arrived, turning lifelong conditions into solvable problems. Now the fight moves to making them affordable. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Bold Effort to Cure HIV Using CRISPR.
item.description: Scientists are making a bold attempt to cure HIV with CRISPR, cutting the virus out at its genetic root. Audacious science for a historic goal. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Old Phones and Smart Software Are Catching Illegal Loggers.
item.description: Discarded phones, tucked into the rainforest, listen for the buzz of chainsaws and sound the alarm. Old tech is becoming the forest's best defender. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Verily's AI Is Diagnosing Diabetic Blindness in Rural India.
item.description: Verily's AI is up and running in South India, diagnosing diabetic blindness where eye specialists are scarce. Sight saved by software, delivered to places the healthcare system barely reaches. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: UPS Got the FAA Nod for Widespread Drone Deliveries.
item.description: UPS won FAA approval for widespread drone deliveries, with health packages first in line. Medicine by air is moving from experiment to infrastructure, and the sky is becoming a supply route. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: The Visor That Diagnoses a Stroke in Half a Minute.
item.description: A simple visor can diagnose a stroke in 30 seconds with 92% accuracy, far above the 40 to 89% of standard emergency exams. Faster answers mean faster treatment, and brain cells saved by the minute. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: SpaceX Took the Commercial Launch Crown From Russia.
item.description: SpaceX overtook Russia as the world's most prolific commercial launcher, reshaping who gets to space. Competition lifted the whole industry. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Teenager Built an AI That Diagnoses Her Grandfather's Eye Disease.
item.description: Kavya Kopparapu built an AI that diagnoses her grandfather's eye disease using a smartphone and a 3D-printed lens. A teenager, a phone, and care in action. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: AI Can Hear a Heart Attack in Your 911 Call.
item.description: An AI system can hear cardiac arrest in a 911 caller's voice, sometimes better than human dispatchers. Every second counts, and now the phone can help. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: The Armada of Saildrones Mapping the Oceans.
item.description: A fleet of autonomous saildrones is mapping our oceans and gathering research data on its own. The wind is doing the driving while science rides along. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: How Robots Are Making Better Drugs, Faster.
item.description: Robots are now helping make better drugs, faster. Automation in the lab is accelerating the path from molecule to medicine. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Robots to Make Robots at ABB's $150M Factory.
item.description: At ABB's $150 million factory, robots build robots. Automation is now manufacturing itself, and the future is assembling fast. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: The FDA Approved the First Blood Sugar Monitor Without Finger Pricks.
item.description: The FDA approved the first blood sugar monitor that needs no finger pricks, sparing diabetics thousands of tiny stabs. Small mercies are still mercies, and this one touches millions of fingertips. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Nanorobots That Swim Through Your Body to Deliver Medicine Are Coming.
item.description: Tiny robots that swim through your body, deliver medicine exactly where it is needed, then dissolve away. The future of treatment may be smaller than a speck of dust. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Gene Therapy Made Deaf Mice Hear Again.
item.description: Gene therapy ferried healthy genes into the inner ears of deaf mice, and they could hear again. A virus doing good, for once. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: ISRO Launched 104 Satellites on One Rocket.
item.description: ISRO launched 104 satellites on a single rocket, a world record set aboard the famously frugal PSLV. India's space program keeps proving that ingenuity beats big budgets. (Kudos level 3: Legend.)

item.title: The Robot With Its Head in the Cloud.
item.description: This warehouse robot doesn't just pick boxes, it shares what it learns with a hive mind of its peers. Every robot gets smarter from every shift. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: The App That Diagnoses Genetic Disorders at a Glance.
item.description: An app can diagnose genetic disorders at a glance, doing in minutes what took doctors 16 years. Facial recognition is becoming a lifeline for rare diseases. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Asked Via a Mind-Reading Device, Locked-In Patients Said "I Love to Live."
item.description: Asked through a brain-computer interface, three of four fully locked-in ALS patients said they love to live. A quiet, profound answer: technology giving a voice to those the world assumed had gone silent. (Kudos level 3: Legend.)

item.title: An AI Recreated a Nobel-Winning Physics Experiment in One Hour.
item.description: An Australian National University AI recreated a Nobel-winning physics experiment in a single hour, learning the Bose-Einstein condensate setup from scratch. Machines that learn like scientists. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: The $1,000 Braille Tablet Made of Microfluidic Bubbles.
item.description: A braille tablet built on microfluidic bubbles promises full-page tactile graphics for under $1,000, a fraction of today's costs. Charts, graphs, and whole pages, finally touchable for blind readers. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: ISRO Launched 20 Satellites on a Single Rocket.
item.description: ISRO packed 20 satellites onto a single rocket and put them all in orbit in about 26 minutes. Efficiency at rocket scale. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Soft Exosuit Is Helping Stroke Victims Walk Again.
item.description: A low-cost, low-tech soft exosuit from Harvard is helping stroke victims walk again. Gentle robotics, enormous human impact. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: The Painting Robot That Didn't Steal Anyone's Job.
item.description: This painting robot did not replace its human coworkers, it transformed what they could do together. A story about robots that lift people up. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: A Brain Chip Gave a Paralyzed Man His Hand Back.
item.description: A brain chip gave a paralyzed man control of his own hand again. Thought became movement, and independence came back with it. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: "For Us, This Technology Is a Game-Changer": Europe's Emergency Workers Turn to Drones.
item.description: Europe's emergency workers are turning to drones as game-changers for rescues and disasters. Eyes in the sky, help on the way. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Sesame Phone: A Hands-Free Smartphone for Paralyzed Users.
item.description: Sesame Phone gives paralyzed users a fully hands-free smartphone, controlled by head movements. Independence, one glance at a time. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: Ford's Driverless Cars Passed the Snow Test.
item.description: Ford's driverless cars passed the snow test, navigating one of driving's hardest conditions. Winter just met its match. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: The Robot Surgeon That Stitches Better Than Humans.
item.description: Johns Hopkins' STAR robot stitches with submillimeter precision, and it outstitched its own inventors. The robot surgeon is setting a new bar for delicate surgery. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: CRISPR Offers Hope for Muscular Dystrophy.
item.description: Gene editing is offering new hope to people with muscular dystrophy. CRISPR research is moving toward treatments for a disease that once had none. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: The Ingenious Way Iranians Beam Banned Data Over Satellite TV.
item.description: Iranians found an ingenious way to beam banned data in over satellite TV. When the internet is blocked, creativity finds a signal. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: Stem Cell Surgery Regrew Eye Lenses in 12 Children.
item.description: Stem cell surgery regrew functional eye lenses in 12 children born with cataracts. Young patients healed themselves, with a little help from science. (Kudos level 3: Legend.)

item.title: The Drone That Maps, Finds, and Detonates Landmines.
item.description: This drone maps, finds, and detonates landmines 20 times faster and 200 times cheaper. A landmine-free world within a decade is suddenly thinkable. (Kudos level 3: Legend.)

item.title: World Energy Hit a Turning Point: Solar Cheaper Than Wind.
item.description: In 2016, solar became cheaper than wind, marking a genuine turning point for world energy. Clean power is no longer the expensive idealist's option; it is simply the best deal. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Joystick-Controlled Robot That Peels a Membrane 1/100th of a mm Thick.
item.description: Surgeons used a joystick-controlled robot to peel a membrane a hundredth of a millimeter thick. Precision beyond the steadiest human hand, opening the door to eye operations once thought impossible. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: The Stem-Cell Bio-Ink for 3D Printing Living Tissue.
item.description: Scientists developed a bio-ink made with stem cells that can 3D-print living tissue. Printing with life itself is no longer science fiction; it is a laboratory reality inching toward medicine. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Rwanda Began Commercial Drone Deliveries of Blood.
item.description: Rwanda launched commercial drone deliveries of blood, turning toys for some into life-savers for others. The country skipped straight to the future of logistics, one lifesaving drop at a time. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Tega: The Squishy Robot Teaching Preschoolers Spanish.
item.description: Tega, a squishy little social robot, helps preschoolers learn Spanish by reading faces and playing along. Proof that the best teachers sometimes come with fur, patience, and endless enthusiasm. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Singapore's Self-Driving Cars Can Be Hailed With a Smartphone.
item.description: In Singapore, self-driving cars could be summoned with a smartphone tap, making autonomy feel ordinary. The future of transport arrived not with a bang, but with a ride request. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: Satellites Can Pinpoint Poverty Where Surveys Can't.
item.description: Researchers found that satellite images can pinpoint poverty in places surveys never reach. From orbit, we can finally see the people the data forgot, and aim help where it matters most. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: The World's First Robot-Assisted Operation Inside the Human Eye.
item.description: At Oxford's John Radcliffe Hospital, the Preceyes robot performed the world's first robot-assisted operation inside the human eye. Tremor-free precision in a space smaller than a coin: a landmark for surgery. (Kudos level 3: Legend.)

item.title: You'll Love Your Robot More If You Assemble It Yourself.
item.description: Research found the IKEA effect works on robots: people who assemble their own robot like it more and feel real ownership. Build it yourself, love it more: a hopeful hint about how humans and machines will bond. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: Digital-Age Donations: USB Sticks for North Korea.
item.description: Campaigners sought USB sticks to carry outside information into North Korea, digital-age donations for a closed country. Sometimes the mightiest technology is a thumb drive full of the world. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: This Man Controls a Robotic Arm With His Thoughts.
item.description: A prosthetic arm anchored directly to the skeleton and controlled by thought alone. Independence, restored by engineering. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Translation Apps Are Quietly Making the World Closer.
item.description: Translation apps are quietly dissolving language barriers, making the world a little closer every day. The internet made the world smaller; translation makes it closer. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: Satellites Are Measuring Economies in Real Time.
item.description: Satellites with cheap cameras and big data are now measuring economies in near real time. A whole new way to see how the world is doing. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: The $70,000 Exoskeleton That Helps the Paralyzed Walk.
item.description: A $70,000 exoskeleton is helping paralyzed people walk, and it is already approved in the US and the EU. Bionic legs, now real and available. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Hi-Tech Agriculture Is Freeing the Farmer From His Fields.
item.description: Satellite steering, drones, and sensor fields are doing the fieldwork so farmers don't have to. High-tech agriculture is freeing growers from the grind, one precise pass at a time. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: Why Gene Editing Has Scientists So Excited.
item.description: Scientists see a future where they go straight to the root cause of disease and repair the broken gene. That is the promise of gene editing, and the excitement is earned. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: The Terminator-2 3D Printer: Solid Objects From Liquid in Minutes.
item.description: The Terminator-2-inspired CLIP printer grows solid objects from liquid in minutes, 25 to 100 times faster than before. 3D printing just got a serious upgrade. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Weavers Turn Silk Into Diabetes Test Strips at a Third of the Cost.
item.description: Weavers turned silk into diabetes test strips at a third of the usual cost. Traditional craft met modern medicine, and patients save. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: The Hand of a Superhero: 3D-Printed Prosthetics Kids Actually Want.
item.description: Superhero-styled, 3D-printed prosthetics give kids hands they actually want to wear, at a fraction of the cost. Prosthetics that celebrate rather than hide. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Paralyzed Man Walked Again on Brain Power Alone.
item.description: A paralyzed man walked again on brain power alone, with a UCI system that bypassed his spinal cord. His brain reached his legs without the wires in between. (Kudos level 3: Legend.)

item.title: How Robots, Drones, and New Disaster Tech Are Saving Lives.
item.description: From robots to drones, a new generation of disaster technology is reaching survivors faster than ever. When every minute counts, machines are learning to do some of the bravest work of all. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Robots and Healthcare: Early Days, Promising Signs.
item.description: A 2015 look at robots in healthcare found early days with genuinely promising signs. Even the first machines hinted at what was coming: robots as helpers in the hospital, not replacements for the humans. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: The Cyborg Cockroach That Could Search Collapsed Buildings.
item.description: Texas A&M researchers wired a tiny microcontroller into a cockroach's nervous system, creating a controllable insect that can squeeze into collapsed buildings. Nature's best explorer, upgraded with a remote control for search and rescue. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A 20-Year-Old Invented a Life-Saving Smart Wheelchair.
item.description: A 20-year-old inventor built a smart wheelchair that could save lives. Youth, ingenuity, and a chair that changes everything. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: Transplant Surgery Got a Paralyzed Man Walking Again.
item.description: Transplant surgery got a paralyzed man walking again. In the doctor's words: this is just fantastic. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Controlling Google Glass With Brainwaves.
item.description: Brainwaves are becoming a remote control for Google Glass. For people with limited abilities, this hands-free tech could do wonders. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: The Nobel for the Brain's Inner GPS.
item.description: The Nobel honored the discovery of the brain's inner GPS, the place and grid cells that map our world. A beautiful reward for decoding how we find our way. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: "Scientists Make Telepathy Breakthrough."
item.description: Scientists demonstrated brain-to-brain communication, sending messages directly between minds. Telepathy moved from science fiction to the lab bench. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: A Robot Will Beam Live Moon Pictures to Your Headset.
item.description: A robot is beaming live pictures from the Moon straight to your headset. The lunar surface, streamed like a live event. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: A Robot That Helps Autistic Pupils Build Social Skills.
item.description: A robot is helping autistic pupils build social skills, working alongside human support as a patient practice partner. Tech that meets kids where they are. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: The Diabetes Patients Hacking Together Their Own Bionic Pancreas.
item.description: Frustrated by waiting, diabetes patients built their own DIY artificial pancreas systems, tuning them to their bodies. Patient ingenuity at its best: people refusing to sit still while the perfect product was still in a lab. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Peek: The Smartphone Eye-Exam Kit That Could End Avoidable Blindness.
item.description: Peek turns a smartphone into a full eye-exam kit, bringing diagnosis to villages that have never seen an eye doctor. Since most blindness is avoidable, this little adapter could end more of it than almost anything else. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Five-Year-Old Got a 3D-Printed Prosthetic Hand for £50.
item.description: A five-year-old received a 3D-printed prosthetic hand costing just 50 pounds, a fraction of traditional prices. Childhood, with two hands to play with: printed, affordable, and life-changing. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: A Swarm of 1,024 Robots Working With No Central Intelligence.
item.description: Harvard's 1,024 kilobots cooperated as a swarm with no central intelligence, each tiny robot following simple rules. A thousand simple robots, one smart crowd: the power of small minds working together. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: The Smartshoe That Gives Directions Through Vibrations.
item.description: An Indian startup built a smartshoe that guides wearers through vibrations, designed with the visually impaired in mind. Directions you feel instead of see: independence, one buzz at a time. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)

item.title: Training Robots to Paint, Build, and Play.
item.description: Researchers are training robots to paint, build, and play, teaching machines the joyful skills, not just the useful ones. A robot that can play is a robot that hints at something more. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: The Rowbot: A Roomba for the Cornfield.
item.description: The Rowbot is a Roomba for the cornfield, fertilizing plant by plant to cut runoff. Small robot, cleaner rivers, smarter farming. (Kudos level 1: Nice.)

item.title: Batteryless Devices That Talk Over Wi-Fi Using Ambient Backscatter.
item.description: University of Washington engineers built devices that communicate over Wi-Fi with no battery at all, harvesting ambient signals. Electronics that never need charging: the humblest, greenest trick in wireless. (Kudos level 2: Bravo.)
